newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Coelba to be privatized Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Coelba to be privatized Thursday.

text.p: A controlling stake in Brazil's Bahia state power utility Coelba is due to be sold Thursday in a closed-envelope auction on the Rio de Janeiro stock exchange at a base price of 975.8 million reais ($903.5 million).
Bahia state is selling 65.64 percent of Coelba's voting capital and will offer an additional 5.5 percent voting stake to Coelba's employees.
The market expects the offering to be sold at a 30-40 percent premium over the minimum price at the auction, which will be held at 1030 local time/0930 EDT/1330 GMT.

"The market is expecting a premium since Coelba shares are already being quoted above the minimum price," said Oscar Salomao, director of consulting firm Maxima which is advising the Bahia state government on the privatization.
Brazil's National Development Bank (BNDES) is offering to finance up to 50 percent of the minimum price.
At least four consortia are participating in the auction.
Privatized Rio de Janeiro power distributors Cerj and Light, as well as Espirito Santo state's private power firm Escelsa have confirmed they will participate in the auction.

Cerj has joined forces with its controlling shareholders Chile's Enersis and Chilectra, Portugal's EDP and Spain's Endesa, while Light has teamed up with its controlling shareholders Brazil's CSN, France's EDF, U.S. firms AES Corp and Houston Power Industries.
Escelsa is in the final phases of negotiating its partnership with U.S. firm CMS Energy Corp, but plans to bid for Coelba even if CMS decides to pull out, according to an adviser to the consortium.
A fourth consortium in the running is composed of Spanish power utility Iberdrola SA, Brazilian pension fund Previ and Banco do Brasil's brokerage arm BB DTVM.

U.S. Florida Power & Light Co and a consortium composed of U.S. companies Central and South West Services Inc, Chase Manhattan and Brazil's Rede may also bid at the auction, according to local newspaper reports.

Coelba is a good buy, according to Salomao, who says the company has already carried out a number of adjustments ahead of privatization which will boost its financial results and improve its efficiency.
Coelba has cut its staff by 1,500 to 4,700 employees over the last three years and has reduced debt to a healthy level, he said.
The company is also in a good position to invest in power generation in the future and serve as a springboard for future power privatizations in the Northeast of Brazil, Salomao said.
Coelba has 2.3 million clients and supplies 56 percent of the electricity consumed in Bahia.
